entries.meaning: To give up a throne, a position of power, or a responsibility that belongs to you. ---
examples: A monarch may abdicate in favor of a younger heir.
Edward VIII abdicated in order to marry an American.
Critics say the agency has abdicated its duty to protect consumers.
entries.русский: отрекаться от престола, отречься; слагать с себя (обязанности)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he abdicated the throne), intransitive (the king abdicated in 1936)

entries.meaning: To help or encourage someone to do something wrong, especially a crime. ---
examples: Anyone who helps abet a fraud can be charged too.
He abetted the robbery by driving the getaway car.
She was convicted of aiding and abetting the escape.
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: abetted, abetting. In American legal English it almost always appears in the pair aid and abet.

entries.meaning: To hate something very strongly, usually because you think it is morally wrong. ---
examples: I abhor cruelty of any kind.
She abhorred the idea of asking her family for money.
He has always abhorred violence, even in self-defense.
entries.contrast: The final r doubles: abhorred, abhorring. Like hate, it is a state verb, so the continuous (I am abhorring) sounds wrong.

entries.meaning: To exist in very large numbers or quantities. ---
examples: Rumors abound about who will get the job.
Wildflowers abounded on the hillside that spring.
Theories have abounded ever since the story broke.
entries.contrast: To name what is plentiful, use abound with or abound in: the lake abounds with fish.

entries.meaning: To wear away or scrape a surface by rubbing against it. ---
examples: Wind and sand slowly abrade the sandstone.
The rope abraded his palms before he let go.
The paint had been abraded by years of weather.
entries.contrast: The related words are abrasion (the injury) and abrasive (the adjective).

entries.meaning: To cancel a law, treaty, or agreement by official action. ---
examples: No president can abrogate a treaty on his own, the senators argued.
The new government abrogated the agreement within a month.
Several clauses have quietly been abrogated since then.

entries.meaning: To leave quickly and secretly, usually after stealing something or to avoid arrest. ---
examples: If the suspects abscond, the bank loses the money for good.
The treasurer absconded with nearly a million dollars.
Two defendants have absconded while out on bail.
entries.русский: скрываться, сбегать (с деньгами); скрыться от правосудия
entries.contrast: You abscond with money and abscond from a place.

entries.meaning: To touch something along one side, or to share a border with it. ---
examples: Their property abuts the national forest.
The new wing abutted the old library wall.
Houses abutting the freeway get the worst of the noise.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (their yard abuts the highway), intransitive (their yard abuts on the highway)
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: abutted, abutting.

entries.meaning: To make one part of something stand out, or to stress a syllable or word. ---
examples: Designers often accent a plain room with one bright color.
She accented the wrong syllable and everyone smiled.
The dish is accented with lemon and fresh mint.
entries.contrast: Accent is the everyday word for emphasizing a detail; accentuate is its more formal cousin.

entries.meaning: To get used to a new climate, altitude, or set of conditions, or to help someone do so. ---
examples: Climbers need a week to acclimatize before the summit push.
We acclimatized to the heat after a few days.
The seedlings are still acclimatizing to life outdoors.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (climbers acclimatize slowly), transitive (they acclimatized the plants first)
entries.contrast: Americans more often say the shorter acclimate; British English spells this verb acclimatise.

entries.meaning: To formally give someone a right, an honor, or a kind of treatment, or to agree with something. ---
examples: The statute accords refugees the same protections as citizens.
The city accorded the astronaut a hero's welcome.
His account does not accord with what the cameras recorded.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the law accords them equal rights), intransitive (his story accords with the video)
entries.contrast: In the intransitive sense it takes with. The fixed phrases are in accordance with and of one's own accord.

entries.meaning: To go up to a stranger and speak to them in a bold or threatening way. ---
examples: Panhandlers sometimes accost tourists outside the station.
A reporter accosted him as he left the courthouse.
She was accosted by two men in the parking garage.
entries.русский: приставать (к прохожему), подходить с разговором; окликнуть

entries.meaning: To make yourself or someone else get used to something. ---
examples: It takes a few minutes to accustom your eyes to the dark.
He accustomed himself to getting up at five.
We are not accustomed to this kind of cold.
entries.contrast: It takes to plus a noun or an -ing form: accustomed to waiting, never "accustomed to wait".

entries.meaning: To be next to something and touching it. ---
examples: The two offices adjoin each other.
A small garden adjoined the kitchen.
They booked adjoining rooms at the hotel.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the kitchen adjoins the porch), intransitive (the two lots adjoin)
entries.contrast: Do not mix up adjoin (to be next to) with adjourn (to end a meeting): the rooms adjoin, but the court adjourns.

entries.meaning: To make an official decision about a dispute or a claim. ---
examples: A federal judge will adjudicate the dispute next month.
The board adjudicated more than two hundred claims last year.
The case is still being adjudicated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a judge will adjudicate the claim), intransitive (the panel adjudicates on appeals)

entries.meaning: To make a food, drink, or drug impure or weaker by adding something cheaper to it. ---
examples: Some sellers adulterate honey with cheap corn syrup.
Inspectors found that the milk had been adulterated with water.
The company was fined for adulterating its olive oil.
entries.contrast: Adulterate is about mixing something impure into a product; commit adultery is about an unfaithful marriage. The two are not interchangeable.

entries.meaning: To let air into something such as soil, water, or wine. ---
examples: You should aerate the lawn in early fall.
He aerated the wine by pouring it into a decanter.
The tank is aerated by a small electric pump.

entries.meaning: To have an effect on someone or something, or to move someone emotionally. ---
examples: Rising interest rates affect everyone with a mortgage.
The storm affected flights all along the coast.
She was deeply affected by the news of his death.
entries.contrast: Affect is the verb, effect the noun: the storm affected flights, but the storm had an effect on flights. (Effect as a verb exists — effect change — but it is formal and rare.)

entries.meaning: To join or connect formally with a larger organization. ---
examples: Many small clinics affiliate with a teaching hospital.
The union affiliated with a national federation in 2019.
She is affiliated with three research centers.
entries.русский: присоединяться, вступать в объединение; быть связанным (с организацией)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the clinic affiliated with a hospital), transitive (they affiliated the school with the university)
entries.contrast: The verb ends in -ayt (uh-FIL-ee-ayt); the noun and adjective end in -ut (uh-FIL-ee-ut): a local affiliate.

entries.meaning: To attach or stick something firmly onto a surface. ---
examples: Please affix a stamp to the upper right corner.
He affixed his signature to the contract.
A warning label had been affixed to the box.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (uh-FIKS); the grammar noun affix, meaning a prefix or suffix, is AF-iks. Third person adds -es: affixes.

entries.meaning: To cause someone or something to suffer, especially from an illness or a lasting problem. ---
examples: Droughts afflict the region almost every summer.
A rare disease afflicted both brothers.
The city is afflicted by a chronic housing shortage.
entries.contrast: A problem afflicts a person, but a person inflicts a problem on someone: arthritis afflicted her; he inflicted pain on them.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something look greater or more important than they really are. ---
examples: Politicians rarely miss a chance to aggrandize themselves.
He aggrandized his part in the rescue with every retelling.
The legend has been aggrandized over the years.
entries.contrast: The common form is the compound self-aggrandizing; British English spells the verb aggrandise.

entries.meaning: To gather separate items or figures together into a single group or total. ---
examples: The site aggregates headlines from a hundred newspapers.
We aggregated three years of sales data.
Scores are aggregated at the end of the season.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in -gayt (AG-ri-gayt); the noun and adjective end in -guht (AG-ri-guht), as in in the aggregate.

entries.meaning: To treat someone unfairly, so that they have a real reason to complain. ---
examples: A ruling like this is bound to aggrieve somebody.
He felt deeply aggrieved at being passed over for the job.
The aggrieved party has thirty days to appeal.
entries.contrast: You will meet it mostly as the participle aggrieved, which acts like an adjective: the aggrieved employees.

entries.meaning: To campaign noisily for a change, or to make someone upset and restless. ---
examples: Workers began to agitate for shorter hours.
The long wait agitated the patients.
He gets agitated whenever the subject comes up.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (students agitated for lower fees), transitive (the noise agitated the dogs)
entries.contrast: In the campaigning sense it takes for or against: agitate for reform, agitate against the tax.

entries.meaning: To worry about a decision for a long time in a painful, drawn-out way. ---
examples: Don't agonize over it — just pick one.
She agonized for weeks before saying no.
He has been agonizing about whether to sell the house.
entries.contrast: It takes over or about. British English spells it agonise.

entries.meaning: To trouble someone or make them unwell, or to be in poor health. ---
examples: Tell me what ails you.
No one could say what ailed the old engine.
He spent the year caring for his ailing mother.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (what ails you?), intransitive (his ailing mother)
entries.contrast: Ail sounds exactly like ale, the drink. The living form is the participle ailing: an ailing economy.

entries.meaning: To broadcast a program, or to state an opinion or complaint publicly. ---
examples: The new season airs Thursday at eight.
The network aired the interview twice.
Both sides have aired their grievances in public.
entries.русский: транслировать, выходить в эфир; высказывать (претензии, мнение)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the network airs it on Thursdays), intransitive (the finale airs tonight)
entries.contrast: Air out (a room) is a separate phrasal verb about fresh air; plain air is about broadcasting or speaking out.

entries.meaning: To retouch a picture with an airbrush, or to remove awkward details from a record. ---
examples: Magazines still airbrush their cover photos.
The scar had been airbrushed out of the portrait.
He accused the museum of airbrushing him out of its own history.
entries.contrast: Because it ends in -sh, the third person adds -es: airbrushes.

entries.meaning: To drop supplies or troops from an aircraft, usually by parachute. ---
examples: Planes will airdrop food into the cut-off valley.
The army airdropped medical supplies overnight.
Aid is being airdropped to villages the flood has isolated.
entries.русский: сбрасывать с самолёта (груз, десант); сбросить на парашютах
entries.contrast: The final p doubles: airdropped, airdropping.

entries.meaning: To carry people or goods by aircraft, especially in an emergency. ---
examples: Helicopters airlift injured climbers off the mountain every summer.
Rescuers airlifted the driver to a trauma center.
Two hundred tons of supplies have been airlifted in.

entries.meaning: To make someone's fear, doubt, or anger less strong. ---
examples: The mayor tried to allay fears about the water supply.
His calm answers allayed most of the criticism.
Nothing the company has said has allayed investors' doubts.
entries.contrast: The y stays because a vowel comes before it: allayed, not "allaid". Its usual objects are fears, concerns, doubts, suspicions.

entries.meaning: To combine two or more organizations or things into a single one. ---
examples: The plan is to amalgamate the three departments.
Two regional banks amalgamated last spring.
The company was formed by amalgamating four small carriers.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they amalgamated the three offices), intransitive (the two banks amalgamated)

entries.meaning: To walk at a slow, relaxed pace. ---
examples: On Sundays they amble through the park for an hour.
He ambled over to the counter and ordered coffee.
We spent the morning ambling along the waterfront.
entries.contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: ambling.

entries.meaning: To make a bad or painful situation better. ---
examples: Cash payments can ameliorate the worst effects of a recession.
The new rules ameliorated conditions in the camps.
Nothing has ameliorated the housing shortage so far.

entries.meaning: To pay off a debt in regular installments, or to spread the cost of an asset over several years. ---
examples: Most buyers amortize the loan over thirty years.
The company amortized the software over five years.
The equipment is being amortized at ten percent a year.
entries.contrast: British English spells it amortise.

entries.meaning: To cut off a limb in a surgical operation. ---
examples: Doctors may have to amputate the foot.
Surgeons amputated his leg below the knee.
She has learned to ski since her arm was amputated.

entries.meaning: To give someone a drug so that they feel no pain, usually before surgery. ---
examples: They will anesthetize the whole area before stitching it.
The vet anesthetized the dog for the X-ray.
The patient was fully anesthetized within a minute.
entries.contrast: American English writes anesthetize and anesthesia; British English writes anaesthetise and anaesthesia.

entries.meaning: To turn or set something at a slant. ---
examples: Angle the camera down a little.
She angled her chair away from the door.
He stood there angling the antenna until the picture cleared.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (angle the lamp toward the wall), intransitive (the trail angles left)
entries.contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: angling. The phrasal angle for (a compliment, an invitation) means to hint for something instead.

entries.meaning: To take control of a territory and add it to your own state or city. ---
examples: Few governments accept any right to annex a neighbor's land.
Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.
The village was annexed by the city in the 1950s.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (uh-NEKS); the noun annex, a building added onto another, is AN-eks. Third person adds -es: annexes.

entries.meaning: To destroy something completely, or to beat an opponent crushingly. ---
examples: One bad quarter could annihilate the company's savings.
The storm annihilated the entire fishing fleet.
They were annihilated 45–0 in the opener.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: uh-NY-uh-layt.

entries.meaning: To put oil on someone in a religious ceremony, or to publicly choose someone as a successor. ---
examples: Party leaders were quick to anoint him as the next candidate.
The archbishop anointed the queen with oil.
She has been anointed the heir to the family business.
entries.русский: помазать (на царство), назначать преемником; умащать елеем
entries.contrast: One n in the middle: anoint, not "annoint".

entries.meaning: To copy someone's style or behavior, usually clumsily or without understanding it. ---
examples: Cheap brands ape the packaging of the originals.
The film aped Hitchcock down to the camera angles.
He got laughs by aping the principal's walk.
entries.contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: aping.

entries.meaning: To shock someone deeply and fill them with dismay. ---
examples: Conditions in the shelter appall every visitor.
It appalled me that nobody called the police.
We were appalled by the cost of the repairs.
entries.русский: ужасать, приводить в ужас; потрясти, шокировать
entries.contrast: American English writes appall / appalls; British English writes appal / appals. Both spell the other forms appalled and appalling.

entries.meaning: To add something at the end of a document, a list, or a file. ---
examples: You can append your comments to the report.
She appended a short note to the email.
A list of sources has been appended to the study.
entries.contrast: You append something to a document.

entries.meaning: To divide something up and give out the shares. ---
examples: The court will apportion the costs between the two sides.
They apportioned the profits equally among the partners.
Seats in the House are apportioned by population.

entries.meaning: To formally inform someone of something. ---
examples: Please apprise me of any change in the schedule.
The lawyer apprised her client of his rights.
Staff were apprised of the decision by email.
entries.contrast: Apprise (uh-PRYZ) means to inform; appraise (uh-PRAYZ) means to judge the value of something. You apprise someone of the news, but you appraise a house.

entries.meaning: To take something for your own use without permission, or to set money aside officially for a purpose. ---
examples: Congress must appropriate the funds before the agency can spend them.
The label appropriated the design without credit or payment.
Critics say the brand has appropriated a sacred symbol.
entries.contrast: Stress falls the same way, but the ending changes: the verb is uh-PROH-pree-ayt, while the adjective meaning "suitable" is uh-PROH-pree-ut.

entries.meaning: To officially accept a plan or request, or to think well of something. ---
examples: The council will approve the budget on Tuesday.
Regulators approved the drug last year.
The loan has already been approved by the bank.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the board approved the budget), intransitive (her parents did not approve)
entries.contrast: Without a preposition it means to give official permission (approve the plan); with of it means to think well of something (approve of the plan).

entries.meaning: To move or curve along the path of an arc. ---
examples: Fireworks arc over the harbor every Fourth of July.
The ball arced toward the top corner of the net.
Lightning was arcing between the two towers.
entries.русский: описывать дугу, лететь по дуге; изогнуться дугой
entries.contrast: Unlike panic → panicked, arc adds no k in standard American spelling: arced, arcing.

entries.meaning: To bend something into a curve, or to form a curve over something. ---
examples: Cats arch their backs when they are startled.
She arched an eyebrow but said nothing.
Tall elms go arching over the whole avenue.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she arched her back), intransitive (the bridge arches over the river)
entries.contrast: Because it ends in -ch, the third person adds -es: arches.

entries.meaning: To cover something with a protective layer of metal or other hard material. ---
examples: The company armors trucks for use in war zones.
They armored the embassy doors after the attack.
Every vehicle in the convoy has been armored.
entries.contrast: American English spells it armor, armored, armoring; British English writes armour, armoured, armouring.

entries.meaning: To stir up a feeling or reaction in someone. ---
examples: Questions like that arouse suspicion immediately.
His sudden wealth aroused the interest of the tax office.
The story has aroused strong feelings on both sides.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse arouse, which is regular (aroused, aroused), with arise, which is irregular (arose, arisen).

entries.meaning: To bring someone before a court to hear the charges and answer them. ---
examples: Prosecutors will arraign the suspect on Monday morning.
She was arraigned on three counts of fraud.
The court has arraigned all four defendants.
entries.русский: предъявлять обвинение в суде, привлекать к суду
entries.contrast: The g is silent: arraign is uh-RAYN. You are arraigned on a charge.

entries.meaning: To find something out for certain by checking the facts. ---
examples: We need to ascertain who was in the building that night.
Investigators ascertained the cause of the fire within a week.
The police have not yet ascertained how the thieves got in.

entries.meaning: To kill or be killed by a lack of oxygen. ---
examples: Carbon monoxide can asphyxiate a person in minutes.
Two workers were asphyxiated by fumes inside the tank.
The gas was slowly asphyxiating everyone in the basement.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the fumes asphyxiated two workers), intransitive (the miners asphyxiated underground)

entries.meaning: To have a strong desire to reach something important. ---
examples: Many of these students aspire to a career in medicine.
She aspired to be the first in her family to finish college.
He has always aspired to something bigger than this town.
entries.contrast: aspire takes to: aspire to a position, aspire to be something. Never "aspire for".

entries.meaning: To attack someone or something violently, with blows or with words. ---
examples: Critics assail the mayor every time the budget comes up.
Reporters assailed the senator with questions about the leak.
The coast has been assailed by three storms this month.

entries.meaning: To state something firmly as true, or to claim a right with confidence. ---
examples: The report asserts that the numbers were changed on purpose.
She asserted her right to speak to a lawyer.
He has asserted his innocence from the very first day.

entries.meaning: To take something in and absorb it fully, or to become part of a larger group. ---
examples: It takes weeks to assimilate this much new material.
Her grandparents assimilated within a few years of arriving.
The team is still assimilating the data from last season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (assimilate new information), intransitive (the family assimilated quickly)

entries.meaning: To shock someone with surprise or amazement. ---
examples: The size of the crowd will astound you.
His answer astounded the whole committee.
We were astounded by how quickly the work was finished.

entries.meaning: To make up for something wrong that you have done. ---
examples: Nothing he does now can atone for that decision.
She atoned for the mistake by working through the weekend.
He has spent years atoning for the harm he caused.
entries.contrast: atone takes for: atone for a mistake, never "atone a mistake".

entries.meaning: To waste away and grow weak from lack of use. ---
examples: Muscles atrophy quickly when a leg is in a cast.
His Russian atrophied after ten years away from home.
The program has atrophied since the funding was cut.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (weeks in bed atrophy the muscles), intransitive (the muscles atrophy)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: atrophies, atrophied, but the -ing form keeps it: atrophying.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something sensitive and well adjusted to something. ---
examples: Years in the classroom attune a teacher to small changes in mood.
The training attuned the staff to the needs of older customers.
She is well attuned to what her readers want.
entries.contrast: Almost always used with to: attuned to the market. American English says uh-TOON, not "uh-TYOON".

entries.meaning: To make something larger or stronger by adding to it. ---
examples: Many teachers augment their income with summer work.
The city augmented the police budget after the vote.
The library has augmented its collection with three thousand new titles.

entries.meaning: To be a sign of how something is going to turn out. ---
examples: Weak sales augur badly for the holiday season.
The early numbers augured well for the new director.
Nothing in that first meeting augured the trouble that followed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the result augurs a difficult year), intransitive (this augurs well for the talks)
entries.contrast: Do not confuse augur, to foretell, with auger, a tool for drilling holes; both are said AW-gur.

entries.meaning: To write a book, a report, or a piece of legislation. ---
examples: Two economists author the annual report together.
She authored the bill that became law last spring.
He has authored more than a dozen novels.

entries.meaning: To change a typed word automatically to the one the software thinks you meant. ---
examples: My phone always autocorrects his name to something else.
The app autocorrected "definitely" to "defiantly".
I sent the text without noticing that it had autocorrected the address.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the phone autocorrected my message), intransitive (the field autocorrects as you type)

entries.meaning: To wait for something that is expected. ---
examples: Three more patients await their test results.
We awaited the verdict in complete silence.
He is awaiting trial in a county jail.
entries.contrast: await takes a direct object with no preposition: await a decision, but wait for a decision.

entries.meaning: To wake up, or to wake someone else up, used of feelings as well as of sleep. ---
examples: One phone call can awaken the whole house.
The smell of coffee awakened something like hope in him.
She had awakened long before the alarm went off.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the noise awakened the baby), intransitive (she awakened at dawn)
entries.contrast: awaken is regular: awakened, awakened. It is awake that is irregular: awoke, awoken.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with a feeling of wonder and deep respect. ---
examples: The scale of the canyon awes almost every visitor.
We were awed by the silence inside the cathedral.
Her performance has awed critics across the country.
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: awe → awing.

entries.meaning: To get rid of something suddenly, such as a job, a show, or a budget line. ---
examples: The network may axe the show after one season.
The company axed four hundred jobs in a single morning.
Three of the projects have already been axed.
entries.contrast: American English also spells it ax; both spellings give axed and axing.

entries.meaning: To talk quickly and foolishly, or to make a soft running sound like a stream. ---
examples: The twins babble to each other for hours.
He babbled something about missing his flight.
A little stream was babbling just beyond the trees.

entries.meaning: To treat someone with far too much care and protection. ---
examples: Don't baby him — he can carry his own bag.
His mother babied him well into his twenties.
You are babying that car; it will be fine on gravel.
entries.русский: нянчиться, баловать, обращаться как с ребёнком
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: babies, babied, but the -ing form keeps it: babying.

entries.meaning: To put an earlier date on a document or a payment than the real one. ---
examples: The contract lets the company backdate the raise to January.
Someone had backdated the invoices by six months.
Executives were accused of backdating their stock options.

entries.meaning: To produce the opposite of the result that was intended. ---
examples: Threats like that usually backfire.
The ad campaign backfired badly.
Their attempt to bury the story has backfired on them.

entries.meaning: To go back the way you came, or to take back something you said earlier. ---
examples: Let me backtrack a little and explain that first step again.
The governor backtracked within hours of the interview.
He has been backtracking on that promise all week.
entries.русский: идти на попятную, отступать от сказанного; возвращаться тем же путём

entries.meaning: To put food on a hook or in a trap, or to provoke someone on purpose. ---
examples: He baits the hook with a piece of shrimp.
She baited her brother until he lost his temper.
The traps had been baited the night before.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse bait with bate, which survives only in the phrase with bated breath.

entries.meaning: To refuse suddenly to do or accept something. ---
examples: Buyers balk at prices like that.
The board balked when it saw the final figure.
He is balking at signing anything before his lawyer reads it.
entries.contrast: balk takes at: balk at the cost. British English spells it baulk, and the l is silent either way: BAWK.

entries.meaning: To grow very quickly to a much larger size. ---
examples: Repair costs can balloon once the walls are opened up.
The deficit ballooned during the crisis.
Class sizes have ballooned since the two schools merged.

entries.meaning: To trick or thoroughly confuse someone, usually in order to get something. ---
examples: Salesmen like that bamboozle people every day.
He bamboozled his neighbors into lending him money.
We were completely bamboozled by the paperwork.

entries.meaning: To hit something hard, making a loud noise. ---
examples: Please don't bang the door when you leave.
She banged her knee on the table leg.
Someone has been banging on the pipes all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he banged the door), intransitive (someone was banging on the wall)

entries.meaning: To send someone away from a place as a punishment, or to drive a thought out of your mind. ---
examples: Old kings could banish anyone who displeased them.
He was banished from the country for twenty years.
She spent the whole flight banishing thoughts of the meeting.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: banishes.

entries.meaning: To put or keep money in a bank. ---
examples: Where do you bank?
He banked most of the prize money.
They have banked with the same branch for thirty years.
entries.русский: класть в банк, держать деньги в банке
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she banked the check), intransitive (we bank at a credit union)

entries.meaning: To leave a person or company with no money at all. ---
examples: One bad season can bankrupt a small farm.
The lawsuit nearly bankrupted the family.
Medical bills have bankrupted thousands of households.

entries.meaning: To admit someone into the Christian church in a ceremony using water. ---
examples: The priest will baptize the child on Sunday.
She was baptized in the same church as her mother.
He has baptized three generations of that family.
entries.contrast: American English spells it baptize, baptized; British English usually writes baptise, baptised.

entries.meaning: To uncover something, or to reveal something private. ---
examples: The dog bares its teeth at strangers.
He bared his arm so the nurse could find a vein.
She has never bared that part of her life to anyone.
entries.contrast: bare sounds exactly like bear, the animal and the irregular verb bear, bore, borne. The silent e drops before -ing: baring.

entries.meaning: To block a road or a doorway with something heavy so that nobody can get through. ---
examples: Protesters barricade the main road every spring.
The gunman barricaded himself in the back office.
Both entrances had been barricaded with office furniture.

entries.meaning: To work as a bartender, serving drinks in a bar. ---
examples: She bartends three nights a week to pay for school.
He bartended at a hotel downtown all summer.
I have been bartending since I was twenty-one.

entries.meaning: To build something on a particular fact, idea, or place as its foundation. ---
examples: Scientists base that conclusion on thirty years of data.
The movie was based on a true story.
The company is basing its new office in Denver.
entries.contrast: base takes on: based on the evidence. It sounds like bass, the low voice.

entries.meaning: To hit something hard, or to attack someone harshly in words. ---
examples: Politicians bash each other for months before an election.
He bashed his elbow against the door frame.
The paper has been bashing the mayor all year.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: bashes.

entries.meaning: To fight or struggle hard against someone or something. ---
examples: Crews battle wildfires along the coast every August.
He battled the insurance company for eighteen months.
She has been battling a cold all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she battled cancer for years), intransitive (the two sides battled over the bill)

entries.meaning: To cry or shout very loudly. ---
examples: Babies bawl when they are hungry.
She bawled through the whole ceremony.
He was bawling into the phone by the time I got there.
entries.contrast: bawl sounds exactly like ball.

entries.meaning: To pull a boat up onto the shore, or of a sea animal, to become stranded on land. ---
examples: We usually beach the kayaks near the point.
A young whale beached south of the pier on Tuesday.
The ferry has been beached since the storm.
entries.русский: вытаскивать на берег; выбрасываться на берег
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (beach the canoe above the tide line), intransitive (three whales beached overnight)
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: beaches. It sounds like beech, the tree.

entries.meaning: To smile broadly with happiness, or to send out light or a signal. ---
examples: The satellites beam the game to half the world.
She beamed when they called her name.
He was beaming all the way through the ceremony.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they beamed the signal to the station), intransitive (she beamed at the news)

entries.meaning: To make a place or a thing look more attractive. ---
examples: Volunteers beautify the park every spring.
The city beautified the waterfront ahead of the festival.
They have been beautifying the old train station for months.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: beautifies, beautified, but the -ing form keeps it: beautifying.

entries.meaning: To be suitable or proper for someone or something. ---
examples: Wear something that will befit a formal dinner.
The town gave the old teacher a send-off that befitted forty years of service.
She accepted the prize with a modesty befitting her age.
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: befit - befitted - befitting.

entries.meaning: To confuse someone so badly that they cannot think clearly. ---
examples: Long legal sentences befuddle most readers.
The magician befuddled the audience with one simple card.
He looked completely befuddled when I mentioned the deadline.

entries.meaning: To feel resentment about what someone has or about giving something up. ---
examples: I don't begrudge her the promotion; she earned it.
Nobody begrudged him a day off after that week.
She has never begrudged a dollar spent on her children's schooling.
entries.contrast: Takes two objects: begrudge SOMEONE SOMETHING (begrudge him his success).

entries.meaning: To charm someone, often in a way that misleads them. ---
examples: Street performers beguile the crowd with impossible tricks.
The salesman beguiled them into signing a terrible lease.
It is a beguiling idea, but the numbers do not work.

entries.meaning: To cut off someone's head. ---
examples: In the play the queen threatens to behead anyone who lies to her.
Anne Boleyn was beheaded in 1536.
Two of the marble figures had been beheaded long before the museum bought them.

entries.meaning: To be necessary or sensible for someone to do something. ---
examples: It would behoove you to read the contract before you sign it.
It behooved the company to settle the case quickly.
It behooves every driver to check the tires before a long trip.
entries.contrast: American behoove, British behove. Almost always used with it: it behooves someone TO do something.

entries.meaning: To decorate something with jewels. ---
examples: The designers bejewel every gown by hand.
She bejeweled the costume with hundreds of tiny stones.
A bejeweled crown sat alone in the glass case.
entries.contrast: American keeps one l: bejeweled, bejeweling. British doubles it: bejewelled, bejewelling.

entries.meaning: To keep going over something long after the point has been made. ---
examples: I don't want to belabor the point, but we are out of time.
The speaker belabored the same statistic for ten minutes.
He has a habit of belaboring details everyone already understands.
entries.contrast: American belabor, British belabour.

entries.meaning: To let gas out of the stomach noisily through the mouth, or to send something out in thick clouds. ---
examples: Please don't belch at the table.
The old bus belched black smoke as it pulled away.
Factory chimneys were belching steam into the cold morning air.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the engine belched smoke), intransitive (he belched loudly)

entries.meaning: To surround someone with troubles or with an army so that there is no easy escape. ---
examples: Lawsuits beleaguer the company on every side.
Bad weather beleaguered the expedition for a week.
The beleaguered mayor resigned on Friday.

entries.meaning: To give a false impression of something, or to show that something is not true. ---
examples: A cheerful tone can belie real anxiety.
The calm surface belied the current running underneath.
His boyish face has always belied his age.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e and keep the y: belies, belied, belying. Not the same as lie (to lie down, to tell a lie).

entries.meaning: To shout or roar in a deep, very loud voice. ---
examples: Coaches bellow instructions from the sideline all game.
The sergeant bellowed an order across the yard.
We could hear him bellowing at the umpire from the top row.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he bellowed an order), intransitive (she bellowed at the referee)
entries.contrast: Not the word below: bellow is BEL-oh with stress on the first syllable, below is bi-LOH.

entries.meaning: To complain on and on in a whiny, annoying way. ---
examples: They bellyache about the coffee every single morning.
He bellyached for an hour about the new parking rules.
Stop bellyaching and finish the job.
entries.contrast: Informal. Complain bellyache ABOUT something. The -y stays because belly joins ache as one word.

entries.meaning: To hit something or someone hard with a swinging blow. ---
examples: Don't belt your brother over a video game.
She belted the ball over the left-field fence.
He has belted thirty home runs this season.

entries.meaning: To complain about something or express sorrow over it. ---
examples: Critics bemoan the loss of small bookstores.
She bemoaned the state of the roads the whole drive home.
Owners are bemoaning another rise in rent.

entries.meaning: To puzzle or bewilder someone. ---
examples: The question seemed to bemuse the witness.
His answer bemused the entire committee.
She watched the argument with a bemused smile.
entries.contrast: Not amuse. Bemused means puzzled, not entertained.

entries.meaning: To measure something against a standard or against what rivals achieve. ---
examples: We benchmark our prices against the two largest chains.
The lab benchmarked the new chip at twice the old speed.
They are benchmarking salaries across the whole industry.
entries.contrast: Benchmark something AGAINST something else.

entries.meaning: To damage someone's reputation or good name. ---
examples: He said the rumors were meant to besmirch his record.
One scandal besmirched a family name that had stood for a century.
She sued the paper for besmirching her reputation.

entries.meaning: To defeat someone in a contest or an argument. ---
examples: Very few players can best her at chess.
The underdog bested the champion in three straight sets.
He has been bested only twice all season.
entries.contrast: As a verb, best means to beat someone, not to do your best.

entries.meaning: To improve something, or to do better than an earlier result. ---
examples: He took night classes to better his chances of promotion.
She bettered the school record by two full seconds.
The program helps families who are bettering their standard of living.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double again: bettered, bettering.

entries.meaning: To cut a sloping edge on a piece of wood, glass, or metal. ---
examples: We bevel the edges so that nobody cuts a finger.
The carpenter beveled the edge of the mirror.
A beveled glass panel catches the light beautifully.
entries.contrast: American keeps one l: beveled, beveling. British doubles it: bevelled, bevelling.

entries.meaning: To put a spell on someone, or to charm someone completely. ---
examples: The old stories say that a single glance can bewitch a traveler.
Her voice bewitched the whole audience.
He stood at the window, bewitched by the view.

entries.meaning: To influence someone or something unfairly in one direction. ---
examples: A loaded question can bias an entire survey.
Early news reports biased the jury against him.
The sample is biased toward younger users.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one s: biased, biasing. Bias someone AGAINST or TOWARD something.

entries.meaning: To travel somewhere by bicycle. ---
examples: They bicycle to work in almost any weather.
We bicycled along the coast for three days.
She spent the summer bicycling through Vermont.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: bicycling, not bicycleing.

entries.meaning: To divide into two branches or parts. ---
examples: Streams like this often bifurcate before they reach the sea.
The judge bifurcated the trial into a guilt phase and a damages phase.
The company has bifurcated into two separate businesses.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the judge bifurcated the trial), intransitive (the trail bifurcates)

entries.meaning: To cheat someone out of money. ---
examples: Scammers bilk older people out of their savings every year.
He bilked investors out of two million dollars.
She was charged with bilking the charity she ran.
entries.contrast: Usually bilk someone OUT OF money.

entries.meaning: To do something to excess in a short burst, especially eating, drinking, or watching episodes. ---
examples: They binge on snacks every time exams come around.
We binged the entire season in one weekend.
He has been bingeing on old detective shows all month.
entries.русский: предаваться излишествам; смотреть или есть запоем
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (we binged the whole season), intransitive (he binged on chocolate)
entries.contrast: The -ing form usually keeps the e: bingeing (binging is also seen). Binge ON food or drink.

entries.meaning: To break down naturally through the action of bacteria and other living things. ---
examples: These cups biodegrade in about ninety days.
The test bags biodegraded completely within a year.
Ocean plastic is still not biodegrading the way the label promised.

entries.meaning: To divide something into two equal parts. ---
examples: Use a compass to bisect the angle exactly.
A new highway bisected the old neighborhood.
The park is bisected by a narrow stream.

entries.meaning: To camp for the night outdoors with little or no shelter. ---
examples: Climbers often bivouac on the ledge below the summit.
The troops bivouacked in a field outside the town.
We spent that night bivouacking under an overhang.
entries.русский: располагаться биваком, ночевать под открытым небом
entries.contrast: A k appears before the ending: bivouacked, bivouacking. Same rule as panic - panicked.

entries.meaning: To vote against letting someone join a group, or to shut someone out of a profession. ---
examples: A single member can blackball a candidate.
The studio blackballed him after the lawsuit.
He claims he has been blackballed by every agency in town.

entries.meaning: To make something black or dark, or to become black or dark. ---
examples: Smoke from the stove will blacken the ceiling over time.
Storm clouds blackened the sky before noon.
The beams had been blackened by years of soot.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (smoke blackened the walls), intransitive (the sky blackened)

entries.meaning: To put someone or something on a list of those to be refused or avoided. ---
examples: Most mail servers blacklist addresses that send spam.
The airline blacklisted the passenger after the incident.
Several screenwriters were blacklisted during the 1950s.

entries.meaning: To speak about God or sacred things with disrespect. ---
examples: In several countries it is still a crime to blaspheme.
He was accused of having blasphemed in the article.
The crowd shouted that the preacher was blaspheming.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he blasphemed the name of God), intransitive (they accused her of blaspheming)
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (blas-FEEM); the noun blasphemy is stressed on the first (BLAS-fuh-mee).

entries.meaning: To make the thin, shaky cry of a sheep or goat, or to complain in a weak, whiny voice. ---
examples: The goats bleat whenever anyone walks past the fence.
A lamb bleated somewhere behind the barn.
He kept bleating about how unfair the schedule was.

entries.meaning: To spoil the appearance or the good name of something. ---
examples: One bad review will not blemish a solid reputation.
The scandal blemished a career that had been spotless for thirty years.
Her credit history is blemished by a single late payment.

entries.meaning: To spoil or damage something badly over a long period. ---
examples: Empty storefronts blight the whole downtown.
A fungus blighted the potato crop two years running.
The town has been blighted by the closing of the mill.

entries.meaning: To cover someone's eyes with a cloth so that they cannot see. ---
examples: They blindfold the contestants before the taste test.
The kidnappers blindfolded him and pushed him into a van.
She sat blindfolded while we hid the presents.

entries.meaning: To hit or shock someone from a direction they were not watching. ---
examples: A question like that can blindside even an experienced speaker.
The layoffs blindsided the entire department.
I was completely blindsided by his resignation.

entries.meaning: To form, or to cause, small bubbles of fluid or air on a surface. ---
examples: Cheap shoes always blister my heels.
The paint blistered where the afternoon sun hit it.
His palms were blistering by the end of the first hour.
entries.русский: покрываться волдырями, покрыться волдырями; натирать мозоли
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (new boots blistered my heels), intransitive (the paint blistered in the sun)

entries.meaning: To swell up, or to make something swell up, with liquid, gas or extra content. ---
examples: Too much salt will bloat you for days.
The payroll bloated to twice its original size.
The app has become bloated with features nobody asked for.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (salt bloats you), intransitive (the budget bloated)

entries.meaning: To strike someone repeatedly with a heavy object, or to force them by crude pressure. ---
examples: Do not bludgeon your readers with statistics.
The victim had been bludgeoned with a length of pipe.
He kept bludgeoning us with the same argument all evening.
entries.русский: избивать дубинкой, забить; принуждать грубым напором

entries.meaning: To make a careless, serious mistake, or to move clumsily without looking. ---
examples: Even seasoned negotiators sometimes blunder.
He blundered into the meeting a full hour late.
The agency has blundered badly on this one.
entries.русский: допускать грубую ошибку, оплошать; брести наугад

entries.meaning: To make something less sharp, less strong or less effective. ---
examples: Tax credits should blunt the impact of higher fuel prices.
Years of bad news blunted their outrage.
The medication has blunted the pain without removing it.

entries.meaning: To talk in a loud, boastful or threatening way that has little behind it. ---
examples: Some candidates bluster when they have nothing to offer.
He blustered about suing everyone involved, then did nothing.
The wind was blustering against the windows all night.

entries.meaning: To speak with too much pride about yourself, or to possess something impressive. ---
examples: The city boasts the largest public library in the state.
He boasted that he had never failed an exam.
She accepted the prize without boasting about it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the hotel boasts two pools), intransitive (he boasted all evening)

entries.meaning: To move up and down with short, quick movements. ---
examples: Empty bottles bob along the edge of the harbor.
The apple bobbed back up to the surface.
Her head was bobbing in time with the music.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the buoy bobbed), transitive (she bobbed her head)
entries.contrast: The b doubles before an ending: bob → bobbed, bobbing.

entries.meaning: To be a sign of what is going to happen. ---
examples: Early sales figures bode well for the holiday season.
The long silence boded nothing good.
Two straight quarters of losses do not bode well for the company.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the silence boded trouble), intransitive (it bodes well)
entries.contrast: Almost always used with well or ill: this bodes well for us.

entries.meaning: To overwhelm someone's mind so that it cannot take something in. ---
examples: The size of the national debt boggles the mind.
The numbers boggled everyone at the table.
It is still boggling my mind that she said yes.
entries.русский: поражать, ошеломлять; не укладываться в голове
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (it boggles the mind), intransitive (the mind boggles)

entries.meaning: To make, copy or sell something illegally, especially alcohol or recordings. ---
examples: Some sites still bootleg movies while they are in theaters.
During Prohibition they bootlegged whiskey across the state line.
The album was bootlegged from a concert tape.
entries.русский: незаконно производить или продавать; торговать контрабандой
entries.contrast: The g doubles: bootleg → bootlegged, bootlegging.

entries.meaning: To start or build something using only your own limited resources. ---
examples: They plan to bootstrap the company for one more year.
She bootstrapped the business with her own savings.
The team has bootstrapped everything out of a spare bedroom.
entries.русский: развивать своими силами, поднимать без внешних вложений
entries.contrast: The p doubles: bootstrap → bootstrapped, bootstrapping.

entries.meaning: To lie along the edge of something, or to be next to it. ---
examples: Four states border Nevada.
Tall hedges bordered the driveway.
His confidence is bordering on arrogance.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (Canada borders the United States), intransitive (his tone bordered on rude)
entries.contrast: In the figurative sense it takes on: bordering on absurd.

entries.meaning: To put a liquid into bottles. ---
examples: They bottle the spring water right at the source.
The winery bottled six thousand cases last year.
All of the juice sold here is bottled on site.

entries.meaning: To weave three or more strands of hair, rope or cloth together. ---
examples: Can you braid my hair before school?
She braided three ribbons into a cord.
The child sat braiding blades of grass.

entries.meaning: To force someone to accept ideas by repeating them relentlessly. ---
examples: Advertising does not brainwash anyone overnight.
The group brainwashed its recruits over several years.
He claims he was brainwashed into signing the papers.

entries.meaning: To divide into two or more parts that go in different directions. ---
examples: The trail branches just past the bridge.
The river branched into three narrow channels.
A wide crack was branching across the ceiling.

entries.meaning: To wave something, especially a weapon, in a threatening or showy way. ---
examples: Nobody should brandish a weapon in a crowded store.
He brandished the letter as proof.
The suspect was brandishing a knife when officers arrived.

entries.meaning: To face something dangerous or unpleasant instead of avoiding it. ---
examples: Thousands brave the cold for the parade every year.
She braved rush-hour traffic to get here on time.
They are braving a storm to reach the island.
entries.русский: смело встречать, не бояться; бросать вызов (стихии)

entries.meaning: To coat food in breadcrumbs before cooking it. ---
examples: Bread the cutlets before you put them in the pan.
He breaded the fish with crushed crackers.
The chicken here is breaded and baked, not fried.
entries.contrast: The verb bread is BRED, exactly like bred, the past of breed.

entries.meaning: To connect two things or to close the gap between them. ---
examples: The program is meant to bridge the gap between school and work.
A single plank bridged the ditch.
Nothing has bridged the distance between the two sides.

entries.meaning: To be so full that the contents are about to spill over. ---
examples: His eyes brim with tears whenever he tells that story.
The creek brimmed over its banks after the rain.
She came back from the trip brimming with ideas.
entries.contrast: The m doubles: brim → brimmed, brimming. It normally takes with.

entries.meaning: To react with sudden visible anger, or to stand up stiffly like short hairs. ---
examples: Some readers bristle at any criticism of the author.
He bristled when I mentioned the deadline.
The roof was bristling with antennas.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: BRIS-uhl. In the angry sense it takes at.

entries.meaning: To arrange an agreement between two sides who will not deal with each other directly. ---
examples: Diplomats are still trying to broker a ceasefire.
She brokered the sale of the entire building.
The deal was brokered late on a Friday night.

entries.meaning: To think about something unpleasant for a long time in a gloomy way. ---
examples: Try not to brood over things you cannot change.
He brooded about the argument for a week.
She sat brooding by the window all afternoon.
entries.русский: мрачно размышлять, хандрить; сидеть на яйцах
entries.contrast: Takes over or about: brooding over a mistake.

entries.meaning: To treat someone with extreme cruelty, or to make someone cruel. ---
examples: War brutalizes everyone it touches.
Guards brutalized prisoners for years before anyone noticed.
Several detainees said they had been brutalized in custody.
entries.contrast: American English spells it brutalize; British English writes brutalise.

entries.meaning: To resist something, or, of a horse, to jump with the back arched. ---
examples: Few companies dare to buck the trend right now.
The horse bucked and threw him into the dirt.
Their sales have been bucking the downturn all year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (buck the trend), intransitive (the horse bucked)

entries.meaning: To move slightly, or to change your position in an argument. ---
examples: The window will not budge.
Neither side budged an inch during the talks.
The seller has not budged on the price.
entries.русский: сдвигаться с места, сдвинуть; уступать, уступить
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I could not budge the lid), intransitive (he would not budge)
entries.contrast: Almost always used with a negative: it won't budge.

entries.meaning: To swell out beyond the usual surface or shape. ---
examples: His pockets bulge with candy every Halloween.
Her eyes bulged when she saw the bill.
The suitcase was bulging at the seams.

entries.meaning: To knock down or clear something with heavy machinery, or to force something through. ---
examples: The city plans to bulldoze the old stadium.
Developers bulldozed the orchard in a single weekend.
The bill was bulldozed through the legislature in two days.

entries.meaning: To do something badly and spoil it through carelessness. ---
examples: A nervous witness can bungle even a simple answer.
The department bungled the investigation from the start.
The rollout was so badly bungled that they started over.

entries.meaning: To keep something afloat, or to lift someone's spirits or prospects. ---
examples: Good jobs numbers usually buoy the market.
Strong exports buoyed the economy last quarter.
The team was buoyed by the crowd behind them.
entries.contrast: In American English buoy has two syllables, BOO-ee, not BOY.

entries.meaning: To load someone with something heavy or difficult to carry. ---
examples: I do not want to burden you with my problems.
The new rules burdened small shops with extra paperwork.
Graduates are burdened with enormous debt.
entries.contrast: Takes with: burdened with responsibility.

entries.meaning: To grow or develop quickly. ---
examples: Interest in the sport continues to burgeon.
The population burgeoned after the plant opened.
A burgeoning middle class is reshaping the market.

entries.meaning: To polish a surface until it shines, or to improve a reputation. ---
examples: The trip was meant to burnish his image abroad.
She burnished the copper pot until it gleamed.
He has spent a decade burnishing his credentials.

entries.meaning: To carry a group of people somewhere by bus. ---
examples: The district buses children across town every morning.
They bused the fans to the stadium in shifts.
Students were bused in from three counties.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one s: buses, bused, busing. The doubled forms busses, bussed, bussing are British.

entries.meaning: To move around quickly and busily. ---
examples: Vendors bustle through the market every Saturday.
She bustled around the kitchen making coffee.
The station was bustling with commuters.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: BUS-uhl.

entries.meaning: To go around something instead of through it, or to skip a required step. ---
examples: You can bypass the form and call the office directly.
The new highway bypassed the old town center.
By bypassing the spam filter, the message reached everyone.

entries.meaning: To shut an animal or a person in a cage. ---
examples: Good zoos no longer cage large animals the way they once did.
They caged the parrot for the drive home.
He felt caged in that windowless office.
entries.русский: сажать в клетку, посадить в клетку; запирать

entries.meaning: To persuade someone gently and flatteringly to do something. ---
examples: You cannot cajole him into changing his mind.
She cajoled her brother into driving her to the airport.
After an hour of cajoling, they finally agreed.
entries.contrast: Takes into: cajoled into signing.

entries.meaning: To adjust an instrument or a judgment so that it measures correctly. ---
examples: Technicians calibrate the scales every morning.
We calibrated our expectations after the first week.
The sensor has not been calibrated since it was installed.

entries.meaning: To take parts from one thing to repair another, or to take business away from your own product. ---
examples: A cheaper model could cannibalize sales of the flagship.
They cannibalized two dead machines to build one that worked.
The new store is cannibalizing its own customers.
entries.русский: разбирать на запчасти; поглощать собственные продажи

entries.meaning: To turn over in the water. ---
examples: Small boats capsize easily in that channel.
The ferry capsized in heavy seas.
Two kayaks had capsized before the guides noticed.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the boat capsized), transitive (a wave capsized the kayak)

entries.meaning: To feel that something or someone matters to you. ---
examples: Who cares what time it starts?
Honestly, I do not care who wins.
She cared deeply about her students, even after she retired.
entries.contrast: The standard American idiom is couldn't care less, not could care less.

entries.meaning: To move fast and out of control, swerving from side to side. ---
examples: Shopping carts careen down that hill all summer.
The truck careened into a ditch.
The car went careening across three lanes of traffic.
entries.contrast: In American English careen is the usual verb for lurching out of control; career in that sense is British.

entries.meaning: To describe or draw someone in an exaggerated way that makes them ridiculous. ---
examples: Critics caricature the proposal as a giveaway to the rich.
The cartoon caricatured the mayor as a sleeping cat.
His accent has been caricatured on television for years.

entries.meaning: To steal a car by force from the person driving it. ---
examples: Thieves carjack drivers at red lights in that part of the city.
Two men carjacked a delivery van downtown.
She was carjacked outside her own garage.
entries.русский: угонять машину с применением силы, отбирать автомобиль у водителя

entries.meaning: To criticize someone severely, usually in public. ---
examples: Editorials castigate the mayor almost every week.
The judge castigated both attorneys for wasting the court's time.
He has been publicly castigated for the remark.

entries.meaning: To remove the testicles of a male animal, or to take the force out of something. ---
examples: Veterinarians routinely castrate male cats and dogs.
Amendments castrated the bill before the final vote.
The bull had been castrated as a calf.

entries.meaning: To cause or speed up a reaction or a change. ---
examples: Enzymes catalyze these reactions at body temperature.
The report catalyzed a national debate about policing.
Cheap credit has catalyzed a building boom.
entries.contrast: American English spells it catalyze; British English writes catalyse.

entries.meaning: To throw or be thrown suddenly and violently into a new place or position. ---
examples: One hit song can catapult a singer to fame.
The collision catapulted him through the windshield.
That role has catapulted her into the spotlight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the crash catapulted him forward), intransitive (he catapulted out of his chair)

entries.meaning: To seal a joint or seam with a waterproof filler. ---
examples: You should caulk around the tub before you paint.
He caulked every window frame before winter.
The seams have been caulked and sanded smooth.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: caulk is KAWK.

entries.meaning: To make something happen, usually something bad. ---
examples: Heavy rain can cause flash flooding in these canyons.
The delay caused us to miss our connection.
Storms have caused millions of dollars in damage this year.

entries.meaning: To stop resisting and give in to pressure. ---
examples: Management always caves when a strike is threatened.
He caved after an hour of arguing.
The company has caved to public pressure and issued refunds.
entries.contrast: It takes to: caved to pressure. With in the meaning shifts to collapsing: the roof caved in.

entries.meaning: To give up power, land or a right, usually because you have to. ---
examples: No government wants to cede control of its own borders.
Spain ceded the islands in 1898.
He has ceded the lead to his closest rival.
entries.contrast: cede sounds exactly like seed.

entries.meaning: To make a relationship, reputation, or position firm and lasting. ---
examples: A trade deal would cement ties between the two countries.
Her second album cemented her reputation as a songwriter.
The win has cemented their place at the top of the league.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone formally and severely, usually by an official vote or statement. ---
examples: The board may censure its own chairman.
Two senators were censured for accepting the gifts.
The committee is censuring him for misusing public money.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse censure (SEN-shur, to condemn formally) with censor (SEN-sur, to cut material out of a book or film).

entries.meaning: To put something in the exact middle of a space. ---
examples: Center the heading at the top of the page.
He centered the vase on the table and stepped back.
The photo was not centered properly, so we printed it again.
entries.contrast: American English spells it center, centered, centering; British English writes centre, centred, centring.

entries.meaning: To bring control of something under a single authority or place. ---
examples: The reform will centralize hiring in one office.
They centralized all customer records on a single server.
Power has been steadily centralized in the capital.
entries.contrast: British English writes centralise; American English uses centralize.

entries.meaning: To fasten or hold something in place with a chain. ---
examples: Always chain your bike to the rack outside.
They chained the gate shut for the winter.
The dog was chained to a post in the yard all day.

entries.meaning: To do something risky and hope that nothing goes wrong. ---
examples: The ice looks thin — I wouldn't chance it.
She chanced a quick look over her shoulder.
They are chancing a two-day drive in that old car.
entries.contrast: The silent -e drops before -ing: chance → chancing, but stays in chanced.

entries.meaning: To describe the nature of something, or to be a typical feature of it. ---
examples: How would you characterize their relationship?
He characterized the meeting as productive.
The season has been characterized by heavy rain.
entries.contrast: British English writes characterise. The first syllable keeps its r: KER-uk-tuh-ryz.

entries.meaning: To hire a plane, boat, or bus for your own private use. ---
examples: The team will charter a plane for the away game.
They chartered a bus to take everyone to the wedding.
We are chartering a fishing boat for the weekend.

entries.meaning: To make someone humbler and more careful, usually after a failure or a rebuke. ---
examples: A loss like that should chasten any team.
The scandal chastened the whole industry.
He came back chastened and much quieter than before.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: chasten is CHAY-suhn, like hasten.

entries.meaning: To make something seem less valuable or less worthy of respect. ---
examples: Constant discounts cheapen the brand.
That remark cheapened an otherwise serious debate.
He felt cheapened by the whole experience.

entries.meaning: To choose only the items that support your case and ignore the rest. ---
examples: Don't cherry-pick the numbers that suit your argument.
The report cherry-picked two good years and skipped the rest.
They are cherry-picking quotes from a two-hour interview.
entries.contrast: Written with a hyphen in American English: cherry-pick, cherry-picked, cherry-picking.

entries.meaning: To add chlorine to water in order to kill bacteria. ---
examples: The city chlorinates its drinking water year-round.
They chlorinated the pool before the season opened.
Heavily chlorinated water can irritate your eyes.

entries.meaning: To chew something loudly and in big bites. ---
examples: The kids chomp through a box of cereal every week.
He chomped on an apple the whole way home.
The horse was chomping at the long grass by the fence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (chomp a carrot), intransitive (chomp on gum)
entries.contrast: Chomping at the bit is a fixed idiom meaning impatient to start.

entries.meaning: To laugh out loud in a gleeful, snorting way. ---
examples: He chortles every single time he tells that story.
The audience chortled at the mayor's answer.
She was still chortling about it when we left.

entries.meaning: To baptize a baby and give it a name, or to give a name to something new. ---
examples: They will christen the baby in June.
The mayor christened the new ferry with a bottle of champagne.
The hall has been christened after the school's founder.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: christen is KRIS-uhn.

entries.meaning: To record a series of events in the order in which they happened. ---
examples: The film chronicles one family's escape from the war.
She chronicled the strike in a series of blog posts.
Their rise has been chronicled in three separate books.

entries.meaning: To throw something carelessly or casually. ---
examples: Just chuck it in the back of the truck.
He chucked the old mattress into the dumpster.
She was chucking snowballs at her brother all afternoon.

entries.meaning: To laugh quietly to yourself. ---
examples: The kids chuckle every time the dog does that.
He chuckled and shook his head.
She was still chuckling about it an hour later.

entries.meaning: To cut away the foreskin of a male, usually for religious or medical reasons. ---
examples: Some parents choose to circumcise their sons.
He was circumcised as an infant.
Hospitals are circumcising fewer newborns than they did in the 1980s.

entries.meaning: To keep something within strict limits. ---
examples: The constitution circumscribes the president's war powers.
The court circumscribed the agency's authority last year.
Their freedom of movement was sharply circumscribed.

entries.meaning: To find a way around a rule, obstacle, or difficulty. ---
examples: Some firms circumvent the tax by moving money abroad.
They circumvented the ban with a shell company.
The software stops users from circumventing the filter.

entries.meaning: To bring a group or a situation to a more orderly and humane state. ---
examples: New rules should civilize the comment section.
Empires claimed they were civilizing the lands they took.
The debate was civilized by a firm moderator.
entries.contrast: British English writes civilise; American English uses civilize.

entries.meaning: To climb somewhere awkwardly, using both hands and feet. ---
examples: Kids clamber over those rocks all summer.
We clambered up the bank to the road.
He was clambering into the back seat when the bus pulled away.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse clamber (to climb awkwardly) with clamor (to shout or demand loudly).

entries.meaning: To demand something loudly and insistently. ---
examples: Fans clamor for a sequel every single year.
Residents clamored for the council to act.
Reporters were clamoring outside the courthouse.
entries.contrast: You clamor for something. American English spells it clamor, clamored, clamoring; British English writes clamour, clamoured, clamouring.

entries.meaning: To make, or cause something to make, a loud ringing metallic noise. ---
examples: The bells clang on the hour, every hour.
The gate clanged shut behind us.
Somebody was clanging a pipe down in the basement.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he clanged the bell), intransitive (the gate clanged shut)

entries.meaning: To make a loud rattling noise by knocking hard objects together. ---
examples: Hooves clatter on the cobblestones every morning.
A whole tray of glasses clattered to the floor.
The dishwasher has been clattering since breakfast.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she clattered the dishes into the sink), intransitive (hooves clattered on the stones)

entries.meaning: To scratch, tear, or grab at something with claws or fingernails. ---
examples: Cats claw the furniture when they are bored.
She clawed her way back into the race.
The dog was clawing at the screen door to get in.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the cat clawed the sofa), intransitive (claw at the door)

entries.meaning: To clean something thoroughly, especially skin or a wound. ---
examples: Cleanse the cut before you put a bandage on it.
The nurse cleansed the wound with saline.
She has been cleansing her skin with the same soap for years.
entries.contrast: Cleanse is KLENZ with the DRESS vowel, not the long ee of clean.

entries.meaning: To close your hand, teeth, or jaw tightly. ---
examples: He clenches his jaw whenever he is angry.
She clenched her fists and said nothing.
He was clenching the wheel so hard his knuckles went white.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (clench your fists), intransitive (his jaw clenched)
entries.contrast: Takes -es in the third person: clench → clenches.

entries.meaning: To reach the most exciting or important point. ---
examples: The festival climaxes with a fireworks display.
The trial climaxed in a surprise confession.
The season was climaxing just as he got injured.
entries.contrast: Takes -es in the third person: climax → climaxes. It climaxes in or with something.

entries.meaning: To make, or cause, a light ringing sound by touching glass or metal together. ---
examples: We always clink glasses before the first sip.
They clinked their mugs and drank.
The bottles were clinking in the back of the car.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (clink glasses), intransitive (the ice clinked)

entries.meaning: To hide or cover something up. ---
examples: Officials cloak the deal in technical language.
Fog cloaked the whole valley by morning.
The project has been cloaked in secrecy from the start.

entries.meaning: To hit someone hard, or to beat or damage them badly. ---
examples: Storms like that clobber the coast every fall.
Our team got clobbered forty to three.
Rising rates are clobbering small businesses.

entries.meaning: To make an exact copy of a living thing, a device, or a file. ---
examples: Scientists can now clone several kinds of animal.
Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996.
He is cloning the whole repository onto a new laptop.

entries.meaning: To thicken into a soft solid lump, as blood does. ---
examples: Blood normally clots within a few minutes.
The wound clotted on its own overnight.
Her blood was clotting too slowly, the doctor said.
entries.contrast: The t doubles before an ending: clot → clotted, clotting.

entries.meaning: To beat someone or something with a heavy stick. ---
examples: Hunters still club seals on some of those beaches.
He was clubbed over the head and robbed.
Police were filmed clubbing protesters outside the gate.
entries.contrast: The b doubles before an ending: club → clubbed, clubbing.

entries.meaning: To gather in a tight group, or to put things into one. ---
examples: Shops cluster around the train station.
Reporters clustered outside the front gate.
The new cases are clustered in three neighborhoods.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cluster the chairs by the window), intransitive (reporters clustered outside)

entries.meaning: To fill a space untidily with too many things. ---
examples: Don't clutter the slide with text.
Boxes cluttered the hallway for weeks.
His desk is cluttered with old mail and receipts.

entries.meaning: To take over an idea or a group for your own purposes, or to bring someone onto a committee without an election. ---
examples: Big brands routinely co-opt the language of protest.
The board co-opted two new members in June.
Organizers complained of being co-opted by the party.
entries.русский: присваивать, присвоить; переманивать на свою сторону; кооптировать
entries.contrast: Written with a hyphen in American English: co-opt, co-opted. It has nothing to do with cooped up.

entries.meaning: To come together and form a single group or whole. ---
examples: Small protests sometimes coalesce into a movement.
Support coalesced around a single candidate.
The story is still coalescing in her head.
entries.contrast: Support coalesces around a person or idea.

entries.meaning: To write a book, paper, or report together with someone else. ---
examples: The two scientists coauthor a paper almost every year.
She coauthored the study with her former student.
The bill was coauthored by members of both parties.
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen, co-author; both spellings are standard in American English.

entries.meaning: To tilt part of the body to one side, or to pull back the hammer of a gun. ---
examples: Dogs cock their heads when they hear a strange sound.
She cocked an eyebrow but said nothing.
He was cocking the rifle when the deer bolted.

entries.meaning: To write rules or practices down as a formal, official system. ---
examples: Lawmakers want to codify the right in state law.
The agreement codified what had been an informal habit.
Those safety standards were codified in the 1970s.
entries.contrast: The -y changes to -ie-: codify → codifies, codified, but codifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To live together as a couple without being married. ---
examples: More couples cohabit now than a generation ago.
They cohabited for six years before the wedding.
She has been cohabiting with her partner since college.
entries.contrast: One t in American English: cohabited, cohabiting. You cohabit with someone.

entries.meaning: To wind something into a ring or spiral, or to take that shape. ---
examples: Coil the hose before you put it away.
The snake coiled around a low branch.
A long cable was coiled neatly by the door.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (coil the hose), intransitive (the snake coiled)

entries.meaning: To invent a new word or phrase. ---
examples: Journalists coin new terms every election.
He coined the phrase in a 1998 essay.
The word was coined long before the internet existed.

entries.meaning: To happen at the same time as something else, or to match it exactly. ---
examples: The two holidays sometimes coincide.
Her visit coincided with the first snow of the year.
The dates have coincided three years in a row.
entries.contrast: One event coincides with another.

entries.meaning: To gather information or pages together and put them in order. ---
examples: The office collates the results every Friday.
She collated the survey answers into one spreadsheet.
The copies have already been collated and stapled.

entries.meaning: To cooperate secretly in order to cheat or deceive other people. ---
examples: Regulators asked whether the airlines collude on prices.
Two suppliers colluded to keep their bids high.
He denied ever colluding with anyone in the company.
entries.contrast: You collude with someone on or in something.

entries.meaning: To settle in a place and take control of it, or (of plants and animals) to spread into a new area. ---
examples: Bacteria colonize the gut in the first weeks of life.
Spain colonized the region in the sixteenth century.
The islands were colonized twice within a hundred years.
entries.contrast: British English writes colonise; American English uses colonize.

entries.meaning: To take something for your own use, especially by force or official authority. ---
examples: Troops sometimes commandeer private vehicles.
The police commandeered a taxi to follow the van.
Our meeting room has been commandeered by the sales team.

entries.meaning: To do something to honor the memory of a person or an event. ---
examples: Each year they commemorate the fire with a moment of silence.
The stamp commemorated the first moon landing.
The city is commemorating the anniversary with a free concert.

entries.meaning: To turn something into a business that makes money, often spoiling its original character. ---
examples: Startups race to commercialize the technology.
Critics say the holiday has been commercialized beyond recognition.
They are commercializing research that took decades to finish.
entries.contrast: British English writes commercialise; American English uses commercialize.

entries.meaning: To carry out something wrong or serious, or to set aside money, people, or time for a purpose. ---
examples: Most people who commit this offense never go to jail.
He committed the same error twice in one game.
The company has committed two million dollars to the project.
